item.research_question: What designing and regulating strategies can optimize the catalytic performance of multicomponent high-entropy materials (HEMs), and what are the underlying mechanisms revealed by theory and experiment?
item.material_system: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (HEAs), oxides (HEOs), layered double hydroxides (LDHs), perovskites, MOFs, sulfides, phosphides, and (oxy)hydroxides; specific examples include PtRuNiCoFeMo nanowires, Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 nanoparticles, AlNiCoRuMoFeCrTi HEOs, and PdCuMoNiCo hollow spheres.
item.processing_route: Various methods including arc melting, low-temperature oil phase synthesis, pyrolysis of MOFs, galvanic exchange reactions, dealloying of Al-based or Mn-based precursors, mechanochemical milling, Ar plasma etching, metal-tannin coordination assembly, sol-gel methods, Joule heating for intermetallic formation, and high-temperature carbon shock synthesis.
item.test_conditions: Electrochemical tests in alkaline media (e.g., 0.5 M H2SO4, alkaline solutions) for reactions including hydrogen oxidation (HOR), hydrogen evolution (HER), methanol oxidation (MOR), glycerol oxidation (GOR), ethanol oxidation (EOR), oxygen reduction (ORR), oxygen evolution (OER), CO oxidation, and CO2 reduction; also tested in Li-O2 batteries and for photocatalytic water splitting.
key_findings: PtRuNiCoFeMo HEA nanowires with 1.8 ± 0.3 nm diameter achieved mass activity of 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1 and specific activity of 8.96 mA cm−2 for HOR, which are 4.1 and 19.8 times higher than commercial PtRu/C and Pt/C, respectively.
NiCoFePtRh ultrasmall sub-2 nm HEA nanoparticles achieved a mass activity of 28.3 A mg−1 for HER, which is 40.4 times larger than commercial Pt/C.
Quinary AlNiCoRuMo nanoporous alloy/oxide system exhibited much better activities for HER, OER, and ORR compared to ternary and quaternary samples, with only 20 at% Ru content.
8-component AlNiCoRuMoFeCrTi HEO showed OER/ORR activities comparable to the quinary AlNiCoRuMo but with reduced Ru content (12.5% in theory) due to a Cr–Fe synergistic effect.
PdCuMoNiCo hollow spherical nanoparticles exhibited higher specific surface area and bi-functional activity for formic acid oxidation and ORR compared to solid counterparts.

High-entropy perovskite cobaltate with five equimolar metals achieved an overpotential of 320 mV at 10 mA cm−2 for OER, with the high configuration entropy facilitating a shift from the adsorbate evolution mechanism to the lattice oxygen mechanism (LOM).
Pt25Pd25Ni25P25 amorphous HEA exhibited 5- and 10-fold higher HER activity in alkaline solutions compared to ternary Pt60Ni15P25 and Pd40Ni40P20 amorphous alloys, respectively.
Five-component (MoWVNbTa)S2 high-entropy dichalcogenide achieved a high current density of 0.51 A cm−2 and turnover frequency of 58.3 s−1 for CO2 reduction to CO.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the random distribution of different metal elements in HEMs contributes to transcendental homogeneity and unexpected synergistic effects that stimulate the kinetic barrier for adsorption/desorption. The 'cocktail effect' and entropy stabilization allow for tunable electronic structures, where specific elements can adjust the local density of states (LDOS) and d-band centers of active sites. Defects (like oxygen vacancies) and strain effects further modulate adsorption energies, while the high configurational entropy can facilitate the formation of oxygen vacancies and shift reaction mechanisms (e.g., to LOM). In ordered intermetallics, specific site isolation and optimized adsorption configurations reduce energy barriers.
item.limitations: The authors state that 'the relationships between the structural effects and catalytic properties of HEMs are still unambiguous', making it difficult to purposely regulate intrinsic surface electronic states. They note that 'we cannot mix any five or more components in one nanostructure without phase separation, especially for these enthalpy-dominated systems'. Additionally, 'the entropy value is usually not related to the catalytic activity', and thorough comparisons of 'best' catalysts are often impossible due to the 'numberless combinations'.
item.future_work: The authors propose that 'a high throughput fabrication strategy is highly needed to prepare more samples for catalyst screening' and that 'developing a novel strategy such as high throughout DFT calculation and machine learning to determine the element combination for a specific chemical reaction is very urgent'. They also suggest that 'for a specific reaction, the phase or element separation may result in a better activity considering the rich interface and possible stepwise reaction on different sites of the heterostructure'.
quotes: The random distribution of different metal elements in HEMs could contribute to transcendental homogeneity, leading to an unexpected synergistic effect to stimulate the kinetic barrier for adsorption/desorption.
The high configuration entropy can facilitate the formation of oxygen vacancies, drastically skewing the OER mechanism from the adsorbate evolution mechanism to the more beneficial LOM pathway.

It should be point out that the entropy value is usually not related to the catalytic activity. The high entropy does contribute to the enhanced stability of the system considering that ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.

item.research_question: How can the active sites of high-entropy catalysts be identified and how can their performance be enhanced through design strategies?
item.material_system: High-entropy oxides (HEOs)/noble metal composites, single-crystal high-entropy metals (HEMs), and multicomponent catalysts with more than 12 or 14 elements
key_findings: The real active sites of high-entropy catalysts for many reactions are still misty, especially for more complicated high-entropy systems such as HEOs/noble metal composites.
Single-crystal HEMs are extremely hard to achieve due to the extensive existence of crystalline lattice strains, lattice distortions, and numerous unsaturated defects.
An equal atomic ratio does not always lead to the highest activity although the highest entropy value is achieved.
The surface states may be completely different from the bulk composites and the surface may be severely oxidized if many active elements are incorporated.
The rich and tunable chemical coordination environment in HEMs makes it possible to incorporate a large amount of single atom catalysts.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that high-entropy design, by incorporating more elements into one system, allows for exploring synergistic effects between elements to enhance catalytic performance (activity and stability) or reduce noble metal content. They suggest that multicomponent catalysts can enhance reaction selectivity by changing the conventional reaction path, and that the tunable chemical coordination environment in HEMs facilitates atomic interaction studies.
item.limitations: The reported so-called best high-entropy (multicomponent) samples may still need further optimization; the surface states may be completely different from the bulk composites and the surface may be severely oxidized; single-crystal HEMs are extremely hard to achieve due to lattice strains and defects; preparing single atom catalysts with ultrahigh loading via a simple method is challenging.
item.future_work: Developing an advanced synthesis strategy for the preparation of single-crystal HEMs and high-entropy materials with precisely controlled nanostructures; developing high throughput synthesis or DFT calculation strategies to screen the most efficient catalysts; preparing single atom catalysts with ultrahigh loading; in situ monitoring of the surface atomic/electronic structural changes; incorporating more elements such as more than 12 or 14 elements into one nanosystem.
quotes: The real active sites of high-entropy catalysts for many reactions are still misty, especially for more complicated high-entropy systems such as HEOs/noble metal composites.
An equal atomic ratio does not always lead to the highest activity although the highest entropy value is achieved.
It is expected that by high-entropy design (i.e., incorporating more elements into one system) and exploring the synergistic effect, we can further enhance the catalytic performance.
